newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OSCE says Chechnya elections feasible.
newsitem.headline: OSCE says Chechnya elections feasible.

text.p: Proposed elections in breakaway Chechnya are feasible despite basic unresolved differences between Russia and Chechen separatists, the head of an international mediating mission in Chechnya said on Thursday.

Swiss diplomat Tim Guldimann, who leads the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) assistance group to the rebel Russian province, told reporters he believed both sides could find an acceptable solution without tackling the sensitive issue of the province's future status.
"If both sides want they can organise (elections) in a way not to wake up sleeping dogs," he told a news briefing after addressing the OSCE's Vienna-based permanent council.

Under a deal struck in August, Moscow and the rebels agreed to postpone the issue of Chechnya's political status for five years in return for a withdrawal of Russian troops from the region. Moscow will keep just two brigades in Chechnya permanently.
Guldimann spoke before news broke in Moscow of the dismissal of Russian security chief Alexander Lebed who negotiated the deal with the Chechen rebel leadership.
Guldimann said Chechen separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, who on Tuesday announced plans to hold local polls in January, had asked the OSCE to monitor the elections.

"This could be an important task for the assistance group but we could only do something if we have the green light from Moscow," he noted. The polls will decide a national leader and local parliament in the province.

It is not clear whether Russia, evidently uninvolved in fixing a date for local elections, would recognise the results. Moscow has not protested a separatist decision, also announced on Tuesday, to form a coalition government.
Guldimann said he could not tell whether conditions for free and fair elections would be established by January.
"But I am positive about the fact that the Chechen side is determined to start the democratic process," he added.
A joint commission of Chechens and Russian officials is also planned to focus on economic and social problems in the aftermath of the bitter 21-month conflict.
While the peace process in the turbulent Caucausus region remained fragile, its move from the military to political arena was positive, Guldimann said.
"It is a question of mutual interests. You don't need legal clarity as long as they (the two sides) don't shoot each other," he added.

The OSCE assistance group has led sporadic talks over the past year between Chechen separatists and Russian officials on ending fighting which killed over 30,000, mostly civilians, since Moscow sent troops to the region in December 1994.

Guldimann said issues of troop withdrawal, elections, the power structure and the hand-over of war prisoners were the key problems still to be addressed. Russian temporary troops were expected to complete their withdrawal in the next 10 days.
"So far the whole development was very quiet and peaceful. I was far more pessimistic a few weeks ago," he said.
